pages.bodyHtml:
The ASNT NDT Level III Basic examination is a 135-question, 4-hour computer-based exam that every first-time ASNT Level III candidate must pass, alongside at least one method exam. It tests the knowledge a Level III needs regardless of method: how personnel certification works under SNT-TC-1A and ANSI/ASNT CP-189, materials and process technology, NDT training, codes, standards and procedures, and a working familiarity with the other common NDT methods. You need 70% to pass. You take it once. When you renew your Level III later, ASNT asks for method exams or renewal points, not the Basic again.

Who the Basic exam prep course is for

Most people who contact us about the Basic fall into one of four groups. The first is the experienced Level II who has been told by an employer that the company needs its own Level III, usually because an outside Level III is signing the written practice today and the business wants that authority in-house. The second is the Level II who is already doing Level III work in practice, reviewing technique sheets, training juniors and answering code questions, and wants the credential that matches the job. The third is the engineer or quality manager with a degree and one or two years of NDT exposure who qualifies for the shorter experience route and needs to learn the certification and methods material quickly. The fourth is the Level III candidate who already passed a method exam years ago under a different employer programme and now wants the ASNT certificate itself.

What these candidates have in common is that they are strong in one method and uneven everywhere else. A UT Level II who has not touched radiography since a Level I course a decade ago will find the Basic's method-familiarity questions harder than the material and certification sections. A quality engineer will find the materials section easy and the method sections hard. Our prep is built around finding that gap early and spending the study hours there, not re-teaching what you already know.

Eligibility: can you sit the ASNT Level III exams yet?

ASNT publishes three education and experience routes for its NDT Level III certificate. All experience has to be in nondestructive testing, under qualified supervision, in the relevant test methods.

EducationMinimum NDT experience ASNT requires
Four-year degree in engineering or a physical science12 months (252 days)
Two years of engineering or physical science study at an accredited institution24 months (504 days)
No college requirement48 months (1,008 days)

If you are not sure how your experience counts, send us your history before you pay any application fee. We read it the way an ASNT reviewer will and tell you plainly whether it is enough. Experience claims are where applications stall, not the exam itself. Our Level II to Level III pathway guide covers how candidates usually document it.

ASNT Level III Basic exam structure

ItemASNT NDT Level III Basic
Number of questions135 multiple-choice items
Time allowed4 hours
Passing score70%
FormatComputer-based, scheduled through ASNT's testing partner (Pearson VUE)
When it is neededOnce, for your first ASNT NDT Level III certificate. Basic plus one method exam gives you a certificate in that method.
At renewalNot repeated. Level III renewal is every five years by points or by method exams.

Four hours for 135 questions is 1 minute 46 seconds a question. That sounds generous until you meet a calculation item on thermal conductivity, or a written-practice question that needs you to hold three clauses in your head. The candidates who run out of time are usually the ones who never practised under the clock. We make timed sections part of the plan from week three onwards.

What the Basic exam covers: the five domains

ASNT groups the Basic content into five areas. The weighting between them is not published as a fixed percentage, so we prepare you for all five and adjust based on your diagnostic results.

1. NDT certification

This is the part most candidates underestimate. You need to know SNT-TC-1A in detail: who is responsible for what, the difference between qualification and certification, how the written practice works, the training and experience tables by level and method, what the general, specific and practical exams are and who grades them, vision requirements, interrupted service, recertification and revocation. You also need ANSI/ASNT CP-189, the standard (rather than recommended practice) version that many US defence and power-generation contracts call up, and where it differs from SNT-TC-1A. Expect questions on ANSI/ASNT CP-105, the topical outlines that training courses are built from, and a working understanding of how a central scheme differs from employer-based certification. Read the documents themselves. Summaries lose the wording that questions turn on.

2. Application of NDT methods

The Basic expects Level II-degree familiarity with the common methods, not just your own. In practice that means knowing, for radiography, ultrasonics, magnetic particle, penetrant, eddy current, visual and the newer techniques, what each method detects, its limitations, the variables that control sensitivity, and when to choose it. A typical question describes a component and a discontinuity and asks which method, or which technique within a method, is most likely to find it. The skill being tested is method selection, the core judgement a Level III is paid for.

3. NDT training

A Level III designs and often delivers training. Questions here cover training programme structure, the relationship between classroom hours and experience, how training records must be kept, and what makes training acceptable under a written practice. Candidates who have trained juniors informally find this section fair. Candidates who never have can learn it in two focused study sessions.

4. Materials science and process technology

This is the largest body of reading. It covers the structure and properties of metals, heat treatment, and the manufacturing processes that create discontinuities: casting, forging, rolling, extrusion, welding, machining, plating and heat treatment. It also covers service-induced damage such as fatigue, stress corrosion cracking, creep and hydrogen damage. The questions link process to flaw: which discontinuity does this process produce, where does it sit, how is it oriented, and so which method finds it. ASNT's Materials and Processes for NDT Technology is the standard text, and it is dense. We break it into weekly chunks tied to the method-selection questions above, so the reading earns marks twice.

5. Codes, standards, specifications and procedures

A Level III writes and approves procedures, so the Basic tests how the documents fit together: code versus standard versus specification, how a code references a standard, what a procedure must contain, and how acceptance criteria are applied. You will not be asked to recite ASME Section V clause numbers from memory. You will be asked what a procedure has to specify and who has the authority to approve it.

A 10-week Basic study plan

This is the plan we start from for a working Level II studying 6 to 8 hours a week. Candidates with a materials or engineering background usually compress weeks 4 to 6. Candidates who have only ever worked one method usually stretch weeks 7 and 8.

WeekFocusOutput
1Diagnostic test across all five domains; read SNT-TC-1A end to endPersonal gap map
2SNT-TC-1A deep dive: tables, exams, vision, recertification; CP-189 differencesCertification question set above 80%
3CP-105 topical outlines, training programme design, written practice structure; first timed 45-question setTimed baseline score
4Materials: metallurgy basics, properties, heat treatmentProcess-to-discontinuity chart, part 1
5Processes: casting, forging, rolling, welding discontinuitiesProcess-to-discontinuity chart, part 2
6Service damage: fatigue, SCC, creep, corrosion, hydrogenMaterials question set above 75%
7Other methods at Level II depth: RT and UT principles and limitationsMethod-selection drills
8MT, PT, ET, VT and other methods at Level II depthMethod-selection drills
9Codes, standards, specifications, procedure content; full 135-question timed mockMock score and error log
10Error-log review, second full mock, exam logisticsGo / no-go decision

The go / no-go decision matters. We would rather you move your appointment by three weeks than sit an exam you are not ready for. Rescheduling costs less than a retake, in money and in confidence.

Key references for the Basic

  • ASNT SNT-TC-1A, the current edition. Read it more than once.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-189, the ASNT standard for qualification and certification of NDT personnel.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-105, the topical outlines for qualification of NDT personnel.
  • ASNT Level III Study Guide: Basic, ASNT's own study guide for this exam.
  • Materials and Processes for NDT Technology (ASNT).
  • ASNT Question & Answer Book for the Basic, useful for practising question style rather than as a content source.
  • ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook volumes, used selectively for the method-familiarity section.
  • ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code, Section V, for how a code organises NDT requirements.

Buy the current editions from ASNT. Old study guides are fine for the physics. They are not fine for the certification documents, which change between editions.

How Atlantis Level III Basic exam prep works

Preparation is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III and founder of Atlantis NDT. Sessions run live online, so you can join from a plant, an office or a hotel room during a turnaround. There is no classroom to travel to.

  • Diagnostic first. Week one is a scored diagnostic across all five domains. The rest of the plan is weighted to what it shows.
  • Live online sessions. Weekly sessions work through the hard material together: SNT-TC-1A clause by clause, process-to-discontinuity reasoning, method selection. They are recorded for the weeks you are on nights.
  • Practice questions in the exam's style. Timed sets built to the Basic's domains, with a written explanation for every answer. The explanation matters more than the score.
  • Method refresh on the Practical NDT simulator. If you have not handled a yoke or read a film in years, the Practical NDT simulator, the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal, lets you run 12 methods in 5 virtual environments. It is a refresher for the method-familiarity questions. It does not replace hands-on work on real specimens, and the Basic has no practical component.
  • Private cohorts for employers. If a company is putting two or more people through the Basic, we run the course as a private cohort on the company's schedule.

Most candidates pair the Basic with one method exam. See the method pages below. When you are ready to plan dates, ask for a Basic exam prep schedule.

Employer sponsorship: why companies pay for the Basic

For an employer, a Level III is a dependency. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer's written practice needs a Level III to approve procedures, administer and grade exams, and sign off certifications. Companies without one rent that authority from an outside Level III, which works but leaves the programme dependent on someone else's calendar. Sponsoring an internal candidate through the Basic and a method exam is how many inspection companies bring that authority in-house.

A sponsored candidate still needs the employer's own specific examination and appointment under the written practice. The ASNT certificate is the core credential. It does not replace the employer's programme. We help with both sides: exam prep for the candidate, and a written practice review so the new Level III has a programme ready to run. If you are planning for a Level III who is retiring, our Level III succession planning page covers the timeline. For a group quote, tell us how many candidates you are sponsoring or use the training enquiry form.

ASNT Level III Basic exam: frequently asked questions

How many questions are on the ASNT Level III Basic exam?

135 multiple-choice questions, with 4 hours to complete them. ASNT lists these figures on its NDT Level III examination page.

What score do I need to pass the Basic?

70%. The same passing score applies to each ASNT Level III method exam.

Do I have to pass the Basic before a method exam?

A first-time ASNT NDT Level III certificate needs both the Basic and at least one method exam. Candidates schedule them in different orders. We usually recommend the Basic first, because its method-selection and materials content supports every method exam that follows.

Do I need to retake the Basic when I renew my Level III?

No. ASNT Level III certificates are valid for five years and renew by points (25 are required) or by retaking the method exams. The Basic is not repeated at renewal.

How long should I study for the Basic?

For a working Level II studying 6 to 8 hours a week, we plan 10 weeks. Candidates with an engineering or materials background can often finish in 6 to 8 weeks. Single-method technicians usually need the full 10 weeks.

Is there a practical exam at Level III?

The ASNT NDT Level III Basic and method exams are written, computer-based exams. Your employer's written practice may add its own specific exam, and some also require a practical demonstration, before appointing you as the company's Level III.

Can I prepare for the Level III Basic online?

Yes. The Basic is a knowledge exam, so live online preparation fits it well. Atlantis runs the sessions live online, with recorded replays, timed practice sets and optional method refreshers on the Practical NDT simulator.

What is the difference between SNT-TC-1A and CP-189 on the exam?

SNT-TC-1A is a recommended practice that the employer adapts in its written practice. ANSI/ASNT CP-189 is a standard with mandatory requirements, and it is often invoked by contract. The Basic expects you to know both and to recognise where their requirements differ.

Does passing the Basic make me a Level III for my employer?

Not on its own. The ASNT certificate requires the Basic plus a method exam. Under SNT-TC-1A, your employer then certifies you as its Level III under its written practice, usually after its own specific examination.

How do I get a quote for Level III Basic prep?

Send your experience summary and target exam window through the contact form. Quotes depend on group size and schedule, and we return them within one business day.

pages.bodyHtml:
The ASNT NDT Level III ultrasonic testing (UT) exam is a 135-question, 4-hour computer-based method exam. You need 70% to pass. Together with the Level III Basic, it earns an ASNT NDT Level III certificate in UT. It tests a Level III's command of the method: wave physics and the calculations behind it, transducers and beam behaviour, calibration, sizing and interpretation, technique selection including phased array and TOFD principles, and the codes and procedures a UT Level III writes and approves. UT is one of the three longest Level III method exams, alongside RT and ET, and candidates often find it the most calculation-heavy.

Who UT Level III exam prep is for

A typical UT Level III candidate has years of Level II shear-wave weld work, thickness surveys and often phased array. They can set up an instrument blindfolded. What they usually lack is the theory behind the settings: why the near field sits where it does, what happens to energy at an interface, how a focal law is built, why a DAC curve falls off. The Level III exam asks about that theory, because a Level III has to write a procedure and defend it to an auditor, not just run the scan.

The other common candidate is an engineer with a degree who qualifies for the 12-month experience route and knows the physics from university but has limited field hours. For them the gap is the practical side: couplant choices, what really goes wrong with calibration blocks, how code acceptance criteria are applied at the weld. We build the plan around whichever gap you bring.

Employers sponsoring UT Level III candidates are usually inspection companies whose work is mostly UT-based (weld inspection, corrosion mapping, PAUT and TOFD scopes on pipelines and pressure vessels) and who want a UT Level III on staff to approve techniques instead of sending every scan plan outside.

ASNT Level III UT exam structure

ItemASNT NDT Level III UT method exam
Number of questions135 multiple-choice items
Time allowed4 hours
Passing score70%
FormatComputer-based, scheduled through Pearson VUE
Also required for a first certificateASNT Level III Basic exam (135 questions, 4 hours)
Validity and renewal5 years. Renew by 25 points or by retaking the UT method exam.

ASNT's eligibility routes apply here as for every Level III method: 12 months (252 days) of NDT experience with a four-year engineering or physical science degree, 24 months (504 days) with two years of such study, or 48 months (1,008 days) with no college requirement. The experience must be in NDT, under qualified supervision, in the relevant methods.

What the UT Level III exam covers

ASNT's UT body of knowledge follows the ANSI/ASNT CP-105 topical outline for the method, at Level III depth. We break it into six study domains.

1. Principles and physics of ultrasound

Wave modes (longitudinal, shear, surface and plate waves), velocity and wavelength, acoustic impedance, reflection and transmission coefficients at an interface, Snell's law and the first and second critical angles, mode conversion, attenuation and scattering, and decibel arithmetic. Expect numbers. You will calculate a refracted angle, a wavelength in steel, the percentage of energy reflected from a water-steel interface, or the dB difference between two signal heights. These questions are free marks if you have practised them and a time sink if you have not.

2. Transducers and the sound beam

Piezoelectric materials, frequency and bandwidth, damping, near field length (N = D²f / 4v), beam divergence, focusing, dual-element transducers, wedges and delay lines, and array transducers. Phased array principles belong here too: element pitch and aperture, focal laws, sectorial and linear scanning, grating lobes. A Level III must know why an aperture choice changes resolution, not just which button to press.

3. Equipment and display

Pulser and receiver settings, gain, reject, filtering, pulse repetition frequency, A-scan, B-scan, C-scan, S-scan and D-scan presentations, gating, and digital sampling. For TOFD: lateral wave and back-wall signals, dead zones, and why TOFD sizes by diffraction rather than amplitude.

4. Techniques and calibration

Straight-beam and angle-beam contact testing, immersion, through-transmission, thickness measurement, reference blocks and their purpose, distance-amplitude correction (DAC), time-corrected gain (TCG), distance-gain-size (DGS or AVG) methods, transfer correction and temperature effects. Questions often describe a calibration mistake and ask what it does to the result.

5. Interpretation, sizing and evaluation

Discontinuity characterisation by echo dynamics, amplitude-based and tip-diffraction sizing, 6 dB and 20 dB drop methods, false indications from geometry and mode conversion, and application to welds, castings, forgings and corrosion. This is where a Level III's judgement is tested most directly.

6. Codes, standards and procedures

How ASME Section V Article 4 (welds) and Article 5 (materials) structure UT requirements, what a written procedure must specify (essential and nonessential variables), technique qualification and demonstration, and the relationship between a code's acceptance criteria and the technique's capability. AWS D1.1's UT clause and API documents that call up UT often appear as context.

A 12-week UT Level III study plan

Built for a working Level II studying 6 to 8 hours a week who has already passed, or is studying in parallel for, the Basic. Candidates with strong physics backgrounds usually compress weeks 1 to 3.

WeekFocusOutput
1Diagnostic across six domains; wave modes, velocity, wavelengthGap map; formula sheet started
2Impedance, reflection and transmission, dB arithmetic50 calculation drills
3Snell's law, critical angles, mode conversion, attenuationRefraction drills without a lookup table
4Transducers, near field, beam spread, focusingBeam-geometry question set
5Phased array principles: arrays, focal laws, scanning, grating lobesPAUT concept set
6TOFD principles, instrumentation, displays, digitisationFirst timed 45-question set
7Calibration: reference blocks, DAC, TCG, DGS, transfer correctionCalibration-error scenarios
8Techniques: contact, immersion, thickness, through-transmissionTechnique-selection drills
9Sizing and characterisation; discontinuities by product formSizing scenario set
10ASME V Articles 4 and 5, procedure content, technique qualificationDraft a UT procedure outline
11Full 135-question timed mock; error logMock score
12Error-log review, second mock, exam logisticsGo / no-go decision

Key references for the UT Level III exam

  • ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook, Ultrasonic Testing volume. This is the core text.
  • ASNT Level III Study Guide: Ultrasonic Testing.
  • ASNT Question & Answer Book for UT, for practising question style.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-105 UT topical outline, to check coverage.
  • ASME BPVC Section V, Articles 4 and 5, and the related SE standards in Article 23.
  • ASTM E164 (contact UT of weldments), E114 (straight-beam contact), E317 (evaluating instrument performance), E797 (thickness measurement).
  • ASTM E2491 (phased array instrument and system evaluation), E2700 (PAUT of welds) and E2373 (TOFD), for the advanced-technique principles.
  • AWS D1.1 UT provisions, as a worked example of code acceptance criteria.

Where experienced UT technicians lose marks

After working with Level II technicians moving up, we see the same weak spots again and again. None of them is about competence in the field. They are about the gap between doing UT and explaining it.

  • Using instrument shortcuts instead of physics. Modern flaw detectors calculate the refracted angle, the sound path and the surface distance for you. The exam does not. Candidates who have relied on the instrument for years find they have forgotten how to do the trigonometry by hand.
  • Treating amplitude as size. Echo height depends on orientation, roughness, beam position and range as much as on flaw area. The exam tests whether you know when amplitude-based sizing is appropriate and when tip diffraction or a drop method should be used instead.
  • Confusing the purpose of the reference block. Is a block setting sensitivity, confirming range, checking the index point or verifying the beam angle? Questions often hinge on that distinction.
  • Forgetting temperature and curvature. Velocity changes with temperature, wedges wear, curved surfaces change contact and beam shape. Level III questions ask what those changes do to a result and how a procedure must control them.
  • Procedure variables. Candidates who have never written a procedure struggle to say which variables are essential, meaning a change requires requalification, and which are not. Writing one procedure outline during your prep fixes most of this.
  • Phased array vocabulary. Aperture, pitch, active elements, virtual probe, focal depth and steering limits have precise meanings. Loose field usage costs marks.

Our diagnostic in week one is designed to surface these early, so the rest of the plan spends its hours where they will make a difference.

How Atlantis UT Level III exam prep works

The course is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, and delivered in live online sessions. You can study from anywhere, with no classroom to travel to.

  • Calculation clinics. The UT exam rewards fast, confident arithmetic. We run dedicated sessions on impedance, Snell's law, near field, dB and sizing until you can do them without hesitating.
  • Weekly live sessions. We work through each domain with worked examples, recorded for shift workers.
  • Timed practice questions. Question sets in the exam's style, each with a full written explanation. Two full 135-question mocks before your exam date.
  • Procedure-writing exercise. You draft a UT weld procedure outline and we review it as an auditor would, because the exam's procedure questions are much easier once you have written one.
  • Method refresh on Practical NDT. The Practical NDT simulator, the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal, lets you run UT, PAUT and TOFD scenarios in virtual environments to reconnect theory with screen behaviour. It is practice only. It does not replace scanning real specimens, and the ASNT exam itself is written.

Ready to plan it? Request a UT Level III prep schedule. Many UT candidates also review our free UT Level II practice questions as a warm-up.

Employer sponsorship for UT Level III candidates

A UT Level III on staff can approve UT, PAUT and TOFD techniques and procedures, administer the company's UT Level I and II exams, and answer a client auditor directly. That is a lot of authority to rent from outside. Companies sponsoring a candidate usually want the credential in place before a large PAUT or TOFD contract, or before their outside Level III steps back.

Remember the two layers. The ASNT certificate (Basic plus UT method) is the credential. Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer still certifies its Level III under its own written practice, usually after a specific exam on the company's procedures. We support both: exam prep for the candidate, and written practice development or review so the new UT Level III has an up-to-date programme to run. For two or more candidates, ask about a private UT Level III cohort or send details through the training enquiry form.

ASNT Level III UT exam: frequently asked questions

How many questions are on the ASNT Level III UT exam?

135 multiple-choice questions, with 4 hours to complete them, according to ASNT's Level III examination listing.

What is the passing score for the UT Level III exam?

70%, the same as the Basic and every other ASNT Level III method exam.

Does the UT Level III exam include phased array and TOFD?

Expect questions on phased array and TOFD principles as techniques within the ultrasonic method: arrays and focal laws, displays, and diffraction-based sizing. Our plan gives each its own week.

Are there calculations on the UT Level III exam?

Yes. Wavelength, refracted angle, near field, acoustic impedance and reflection, and decibel calculations are all fair game. Practise them until they are routine.

Can I bring a calculator or formula sheet?

Testing-centre rules on calculators and reference material are set by ASNT and its testing provider and can change. Check the current candidate instructions when you schedule. Our plan assumes you know the core formulas from memory.

How long should I study for UT Level III?

We plan 12 weeks at 6 to 8 hours a week for a working UT Level II. Candidates who are strong in physics or who have recently taught UT often need less.

Do I need to pass the Basic first?

You need both the Basic and the UT method exam for your first ASNT Level III certificate. Many candidates sit the Basic first. Others study both in parallel over about five months.

How do I renew a UT Level III certificate?

Every five years, either by documenting 25 renewal points or by retaking the UT method exam.

Can UT Level III prep be done fully online?

Yes. The exam is a written, computer-based test, so the preparation runs live online. The Practical NDT simulator is available for method refresh, but it is a supplement to field experience, not a substitute.

Can my employer get a group quote?

Yes. Tell us the number of candidates and your target exam window. We quote private cohorts within one business day.

pages.bodyHtml:
The ASNT NDT Level III radiographic testing (RT) exam is a 135-question, 4-hour computer-based method exam. You need 70% to pass. Together with the Level III Basic, it earns an ASNT NDT Level III certificate in RT. It tests the theory behind every exposure: how X-rays and gamma rays are produced and absorbed, exposure and unsharpness calculations, image quality indicators and sensitivity, film, computed and digital radiography, interpretation of discontinuities, radiation safety, and the codes and procedures an RT Level III approves. RT, UT and ET are the longest of the Level III method exams.

Who RT Level III exam prep is for

Most RT Level III candidates are experienced film interpreters. They have read thousands of weld radiographs on pipelines, refinery piping or pressure vessels and they know a slag line from lack of fusion at a glance. Where they tend to be rusty is the physics and arithmetic that decide an exposure: why a change in source-to-film distance changes exposure time by the square of the ratio, how half-value layers combine, how to pick a source for a given thickness, how geometric unsharpness limits what an IQI can show. A Level III has to set techniques and defend them. The exam checks that.

A second group is increasingly common: technicians who came up on computed radiography (CR) or digital detector arrays (DDA) and have less film experience. The exam still expects film knowledge, including processing, density and film characteristics, alongside digital concepts. We rebalance the plan for those candidates.

Employers sponsoring RT Level III candidates are usually radiography contractors, pipeline inspection companies and fabricators with in-house RT bays. For them a Level III is also a radiation safety asset, because much of the procedure and technique authority in a licensed radiography programme runs through the same senior person, alongside the licence's named radiation safety officer.

ASNT Level III RT exam structure

ItemASNT NDT Level III RT method exam
Number of questions135 multiple-choice items
Time allowed4 hours
Passing score70%
FormatComputer-based, scheduled through Pearson VUE
Also required for a first certificateASNT Level III Basic exam
Validity and renewal5 years. Renew by 25 points or by retaking the RT method exam.

ASNT's eligibility routes are the same for every method: 12 months (252 days) of NDT experience with a four-year engineering or physical science degree, 24 months (504 days) with two years of such study, or 48 months (1,008 days) with no college requirement.

What the RT Level III exam covers

We organise the ASNT RT body of knowledge, which follows the ANSI/ASNT CP-105 radiographic topical outline at Level III depth, into six domains.

1. Radiation physics

Atomic structure, the electromagnetic spectrum, X-ray production in a tube (tube current, voltage, target material, focal spot), continuous and characteristic spectra, gamma-ray sources and decay, half-life, activity and specific activity, and the interaction of radiation with matter: photoelectric absorption, Compton scattering and pair production. Expect questions on how kilovoltage changes penetration and contrast, and on source decay calculations.

2. Exposure and geometry

The inverse square law, exposure factor and the milliampere-minutes or curie-minutes relationship, half-value and tenth-value layers, equivalence factors between materials, exposure charts, and geometric unsharpness (Ug = Fd/D). Geometry questions also cover distortion, magnification, and the single-wall and double-wall techniques for pipe. You will calculate a new exposure time after a distance change, the decay of an Ir-192 source over several half-lives, or the minimum source-to-object distance for a given unsharpness limit.

3. Image quality and recording media

Film characteristics (speed, graininess, contrast, characteristic curves), film density and its measurement, screens, film processing and its faults, and the digital side: computed radiography phosphor plates, digital detector arrays, basic spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio and contrast sensitivity. Image quality indicators are central: hole-type and wire-type IQIs, placement, source-side versus film-side, and what the essential hole or wire tells you about sensitivity.

4. Techniques and special applications

Weld, casting and forging techniques, panoramic exposures, double-wall single-image and double-wall double-image shots for pipe, multiple-film techniques for thickness ranges, real-time radiography, and neutron radiography principles. Questions often ask which technique fits a geometry and why.

5. Interpretation and evaluation

Recognising discontinuities by product form (porosity, slag, incomplete fusion and penetration, cracks, undercut, shrinkage, gas voids, inclusions), telling artefacts from real indications (processing marks, pressure marks, static, screen defects), and applying acceptance criteria correctly. This section rewards Level IIs who have read a lot of film, provided they can explain their calls.

6. Radiation safety, codes and procedures

Dose units and limits, time, distance and shielding, survey instruments and their calibration, and the US regulatory structure (NRC rules in 10 CFR Part 20 and Part 34, and Agreement State programmes). Also procedure content and the way ASME Section V Article 2 and its referenced standards structure RT requirements.

A 12-week RT Level III study plan

WeekFocusOutput
1Diagnostic; atomic structure, spectrum, X-ray tube principlesGap map; formula sheet started
2Gamma sources, decay, half-life and activity calculations30 decay drills
3Interaction with matter; attenuation, HVL and TVL, scatterAttenuation question set
4Inverse square law, exposure factors, exposure charts, equivalence50 exposure drills
5Geometric unsharpness, distortion, pipe techniquesGeometry scenario set
6Film: characteristic curves, density, screens, processing faultsFirst timed 45-question set
7CR and DDA: resolution, SNR, contrast sensitivity; IQIsDigital concepts set
8Interpretation: welds, castings, artefactsInterpretation drill set
9Radiation safety: units, limits, surveys, 10 CFR 20 and 34 conceptsSafety question set
10ASME V Article 2, procedure content, technique sheetsDraft RT technique sheet reviewed
11Full 135-question timed mock; error logMock score
12Error-log review, second mock, logisticsGo / no-go decision

Key references for the RT Level III exam

  • ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook, Radiographic Testing volume.
  • ASNT Level III Study Guide: Radiographic Testing.
  • ASNT Question & Answer Book for RT.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-105 RT topical outline.
  • ASME BPVC Section V, Article 2 and the SE standards referenced from Article 22.
  • ASTM E94 (guide for radiographic examination), E1742 (radiographic examination practice), E747 (wire IQIs) and E1025 (hole-type IQIs).
  • ASTM E2033 (computed radiography) and E2698 (digital detector arrays) for the digital content.
  • US NRC 10 CFR Part 20 and Part 34, for radiation protection and industrial radiography concepts.

Where experienced RT technicians lose marks

  • Exposure arithmetic under time pressure. Combining a distance change, a source decay and a film-speed change in one question is routine for the exam and rare in the field, where exposure calculators do it.
  • Unsharpness versus sensitivity. Candidates confuse what geometric unsharpness, film graininess and scatter each do to the image, and which control fixes which problem.
  • IQI rules. Placement, selection by thickness, source-side versus film-side, and shims. The exam tests the logic behind them, not just the table lookup.
  • Digital vocabulary. Basic spatial resolution, normalised SNR and bad-pixel maps have precise meanings that film-trained candidates often blur.
  • Safety numbers. Dose units and conversions (rem and sievert, R/h and Sv/h) and the inverse square law applied to boundaries are frequent, simple and easy to miss if unpractised.

Film and digital: how to study both

Treat film and digital radiography as two recording systems that share the same physics. Source, geometry, scatter control and IQIs work the same way. What changes is how the image is captured and judged. Film questions ask about density, film speed and class, processing chemistry and viewing conditions. Digital questions ask about phosphor plate readout, detector calibration, basic spatial resolution, signal-to-noise ratio and contrast sensitivity, and how image processing can help or mislead an interpreter. Learn the shared physics once, then learn each system's quality measures side by side. That halves the reading and makes comparison questions straightforward.

What an RT Level III does, and how the exam maps to it

An RT Level III's working week explains the exam's weighting. Technique development means choosing between X-ray and a gamma source for a given thickness and access, setting source-to-film distance against the unsharpness limit, choosing film class or detector, selecting and placing IQIs, and planning the shots needed for full coverage of a circumferential weld. That is the geometry, exposure and image-quality content. Procedure and technique-sheet approval means documenting those choices so that any Level II can repeat them and an auditor can check them against ASME Section V Article 2 or the client's specification. Image review means acting as the final interpreter on disputed indications and artefacts, and signing reader sheets. That is the interpretation content. Digital transition is now part of many roles: qualifying a CR or DDA technique against film, and setting the digital image-quality requirements. Safety culture means working with the radiation safety officer on survey practice, boundaries and dose control, which is why safety content sits on a method exam. Finally, the Level III prepares and grades the company's RT Level I and II exams and signs off training records under the written practice. Studying with those duties in mind turns a long reading list into a set of decisions you will actually make.

How Atlantis RT Level III exam prep works

The course is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, in live online sessions. There is no classroom to travel to and no radiation exposure involved in preparing.

  • Exposure and decay clinics until the arithmetic is automatic.
  • Interpretation sessions on real-world discontinuity examples, working through the reasoning a Level III uses to accept, reject or call for another shot.
  • Timed practice questions with explanations, and two full 135-question mocks.
  • Technique-sheet review: you draft an RT technique sheet and we review it against ASME Section V Article 2.
  • Practical NDT simulator: Practical NDT, the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal, includes radiographic scenarios across 5 virtual environments for method refresh, with no radiation involved. It is practice only and does not replace the field experience your application must document.

Request an RT Level III prep schedule, or warm up with our free RT Level II practice questions.

Employer sponsorship for RT Level III candidates

An RT Level III on staff can approve techniques and procedures, grade the company's RT Level I and II exams, and answer client questions about film or digital image quality directly. For radiography contractors, having that authority in-house also simplifies audits. The ASNT certificate is the credential. Under SNT-TC-1A your employer still certifies you as Level III under its written practice. We support the candidate's exam prep and the company's written practice. For two or more candidates, ask about a private RT Level III cohort or use the training enquiry form.

ASNT Level III RT exam: frequently asked questions

How many questions are on the ASNT Level III RT exam?

135 multiple-choice questions in 4 hours, per ASNT's NDT Level III examination listing.

What is the passing score?

70%, the same as the Basic and the other Level III method exams.

Does the RT Level III exam cover digital radiography?

Expect computed radiography and digital detector array concepts alongside film. Our plan gives digital RT a dedicated week.

Is radiation safety on the Level III RT exam?

Yes. Dose units and limits, time, distance and shielding, survey instruments and the US regulatory structure all appear. The ASNT certificate is not a radiographer's licence or a radiation safety officer qualification. Those come from state or NRC requirements.

Are there calculations?

Yes, and plenty: inverse square law, exposure factors, source decay, half-value layers and geometric unsharpness.

How long should I study for RT Level III?

We plan 12 weeks at 6 to 8 hours a week. Film-heavy interpreters usually spend more time on physics. Digital-first candidates spend more on film.

Do I need the Basic too?

Yes. A first ASNT NDT Level III certificate needs the Basic plus at least one method exam.

How is an RT Level III certificate renewed?

Every five years, by 25 renewal points or by retaking the RT method exam.

Can RT Level III prep be done online?

Yes. The exam is written and computer-based, so preparation runs live online. The Practical NDT simulator is there for method refresh without any radiation exposure.

How does an employer get a quote?

Send the number of candidates and target dates. We quote private cohorts within one business day.

pages.bodyHtml:
The ASNT NDT Level III magnetic particle testing (MT) exam is a 90-question, 2-hour computer-based method exam. You need 70% to pass. Combined with the Level III Basic, it earns an ASNT NDT Level III certificate in MT. It tests the magnetism theory behind every shot: ferromagnetism and the hysteresis loop, how current type and technique decide field direction and depth, how field adequacy is verified, how particles, carriers and lighting affect sensitivity, demagnetisation, interpretation, and the codes and procedures an MT Level III writes and approves. MT is one of the shorter Level III method exams, but its theory is deeper than most Level IIs expect.

Who MT Level III exam prep is for

MT is very often a second or third Level III method. A candidate who has passed the Basic and a UT or RT method exam adds MT and PT because an employer's written practice needs a Level III for every method the company performs, and surface methods are performed everywhere: weld inspection in fabrication shops, in-service crack checks on refinery equipment, forgings and castings in manufacturing, and components in aerospace and rail.

Candidates also come from wet horizontal bench work in manufacturing, where they have run coil shots and head shots thousands of times but rarely had to explain why a given amperage was chosen. Others come from field yoke work on welds and have little bench experience at all. Both need to cover the side they lack. The exam treats bench, portable, stationary and specialised techniques as equally fair game.

ASNT Level III MT exam structure

ItemASNT NDT Level III MT method exam
Number of questions90 multiple-choice items
Time allowed2 hours
Passing score70%
FormatComputer-based, scheduled through Pearson VUE
Also required for a first certificateASNT Level III Basic exam (135 questions, 4 hours)
Validity and renewal5 years. Renew by 25 points or by retaking the MT method exam.

Ninety questions in 120 minutes is 80 seconds a question, less time per item than the Basic or UT. MT questions are usually short, but candidates who stop to reason out every current-type question from first principles run short. Speed comes from knowing the relationships cold. Eligibility follows ASNT's three routes: 12 months (252 days) of NDT experience with a four-year engineering or physical science degree, 24 months (504 days) with two years of study, or 48 months (1,008 days) with no college requirement.

What the MT Level III exam covers

We organise the ASNT MT body of knowledge, which follows the ANSI/ASNT CP-105 magnetic particle topical outline at Level III depth, into six domains.

1. Principles of magnetism

Ferromagnetic, paramagnetic and diamagnetic materials, magnetic domains, flux density (B) and magnetising force (H), permeability and reluctance, the hysteresis loop with retentivity, residual magnetism, coercive force and saturation, and leakage fields at discontinuities. Expect questions that read a hysteresis curve and ask what a material will do, such as why a high-retentivity steel suits the residual method and a low-carbon steel does not.

2. Magnetising currents and their effects

Alternating current, half-wave rectified and full-wave rectified current, and direct current. How each behaves at depth (skin effect), why AC gives particle mobility and good surface sensitivity, why HWDC is favoured for near-surface detection with dry powder, and how current type affects demagnetisation. This is one of the most heavily tested areas.

3. Techniques and field direction

Longitudinal magnetisation with coils (fill factor, L/D ratio), circular magnetisation with head shots, central conductors and prods, yokes, multidirectional equipment, continuous versus residual methods, and the rule that a discontinuity shows best when it lies across the field. A Level III must design coverage: which shots, in which directions, at what current, to find discontinuities of any orientation on a given part.

4. Field adequacy and verification

Hall-effect meters and tangential field measurement, quantitative quality indicators and shims, pie gauges and their limits, and the amperage rules of thumb found in the governing standards. Know what each indicator actually proves, and what it does not.

5. Particles, carriers, lighting and demagnetisation

Dry versus wet, visible versus fluorescent, particle size and shape, carrier fluids, concentration checks by settling test, contamination, UV-A intensity and ambient visible light limits for fluorescent inspection, and white-light requirements for visible inspection. Also demagnetisation: why and when it is required, reversing-and-decreasing methods, and how residual field is checked.

6. Interpretation, codes and procedures

Relevant, non-relevant and false indications, discontinuities by product form and process, and how acceptance criteria are applied. Procedure content, the role of ASTM E1444 and E709, ASME Section V Article 7, and AWS D1.1 provisions.

A 6-week MT Level III study plan

Built for a candidate studying 6 to 8 hours a week who has passed the Basic or is taking MT as an additional method.

WeekFocusOutput
1Diagnostic; magnetism fundamentals, B-H relationship, hysteresisGap map; hysteresis questions above 80%
2Current types, skin effect, continuous versus residualCurrent-selection drills
3Coils, head shots, central conductors, prods, yokes; coverage designShot plan for a sample part
4Field verification, particles, carriers, lighting, demagnetisation; first timed setTimed 45-question score
5Interpretation; ASTM E1444, E709, ASME V Article 7; procedure contentDraft MT procedure outline reviewed
6Full 90-question timed mock, error-log review, second mockGo / no-go decision

Key references for the MT Level III exam

  • ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook, Magnetic Particle Testing volume.
  • ASNT Level III Study Guide: Magnetic Particle Testing.
  • ASNT Question & Answer Book for MT.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-105 MT topical outline.
  • ASTM E1444 (standard practice for magnetic particle testing) and ASTM E709 (guide for magnetic particle testing).
  • ASME BPVC Section V, Article 7, with its referenced SE standards.
  • AWS D1.1 MT provisions, as an example of code acceptance criteria for welds.

Where experienced MT technicians lose marks

  • Current type questions. Mixing up which current gives the deepest penetration, which gives the best mobility, and which is hardest to demagnetise is the most common error we see.
  • Field direction logic. Circular fields detect longitudinal discontinuities. Longitudinal fields detect transverse ones. Under exam pressure candidates reverse it.
  • Coil maths. L/D ratio, fill factor and ampere-turns appear as calculation items. Bench technicians often use a posted technique chart and never compute them.
  • Indicator limits. A pie gauge shows field direction, not adequate strength. Candidates who treat indicators as proof of adequacy lose marks.
  • Lighting numbers and conditions. UV-A intensity, ambient light limits and warm-up time for lamps are simple facts that are easy to forget.
  • Non-relevant indications. Magnetic writing, changes of section, permeability boundaries and heat-affected zones. The exam tests whether you can tell them from real discontinuities and explain why.

What an MT Level III actually does, and why the exam asks what it asks

The exam content makes more sense once you look at the job. An MT Level III in an inspection company or a manufacturing plant is responsible for decisions that a Level II follows but rarely makes.

Technique development. For a new part number or a new weld configuration, the Level III decides the magnetising technique, the current type, the amperage or ampere-turns, the shot sequence needed for coverage in two directions, and whether the continuous or residual method applies. That is why the exam spends so much time on current behaviour, coil relationships and field direction.

Procedure approval. The Level III writes or approves the procedure that fixes those choices, cites the governing standard, sets particle and lighting requirements, and defines acceptance criteria. When a client's auditor asks why a yoke is acceptable for a given thickness, or why a head shot was chosen over a central conductor, it is the Level III who answers.

Equipment and material control. A Level III sets up and audits the checks that keep a programme honest: ammeter accuracy checks on stationary units, yoke dead-weight lift tests, timer and quick-break checks, bath concentration by settling test, bath contamination checks, and UV-A and ambient light measurements. Exam questions on these checks are not trivia. They test whether you know what each check protects against.

Examinations and training. Under the employer's written practice, the Level III prepares, administers and grades the MT Level I and II general, specific and practical examinations, and signs off training records. Knowing the method well enough to write fair questions is part of the role.

Disposition of indications. When a Level II is unsure whether an indication is relevant, such as a sharp change of section, a heat-affected zone boundary or magnetic writing, the call comes up to the Level III, who has to explain it in writing.

Audit response. When a client or registrar audits the programme, the MT Level III shows how techniques were qualified, how equipment checks are scheduled and recorded, and how personnel were examined. A candidate who can explain those records clearly is ready for most of the exam's procedure and control questions.

Preparing with the job in mind makes the reading stick. Every topic in the plan above maps to one of these responsibilities.

How Atlantis MT Level III exam prep works

The course is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, in live online sessions you can join from anywhere, recorded for shift workers.

  • Theory sessions on the B-H relationship, current behaviour and field direction, the areas that carry most of the marks.
  • Coverage-design exercises: you plan the shots for sample components and we check your reasoning.
  • Timed practice questions built to the 90-question, 2-hour format, with written explanations, plus two full mocks.
  • Procedure review of an MT procedure outline against ASTM E1444 and ASME Section V Article 7.
  • Method refresh on Practical NDT: the Practical NDT simulator, the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal, includes magnetic particle scenarios, useful if you have been in a supervisory role and away from the bench. It is practice only and does not replace hands-on work on real parts.

Request an MT Level III prep schedule. Many candidates pair MT with Level III PT, and we run the two back to back.

Employer sponsorship for MT Level III candidates

Adding MT to an existing Level III's methods is one of the most cost-effective moves a company can make. It closes a gap in the written practice for a method that is performed on almost every job. The ASNT certificate is the credential. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer still certifies its Level III under its own written practice, usually with a specific exam on company procedures. We support both the candidate's preparation and the company's written practice. For group or back-to-back MT and PT preparation, ask for a combined cohort quote or use the training enquiry form.

ASNT Level III MT exam: frequently asked questions

How many questions are on the ASNT Level III MT exam?

90 multiple-choice questions in 2 hours, per ASNT's Level III examination listing.

What is the passing score?

70%.

Is the MT Level III exam easier than UT or RT?

It is shorter, with 90 questions in 2 hours against 135 in 4. It is not shallow. Magnetism theory, current behaviour and field design are tested at a depth most Level IIs have never needed.

Can I take MT as my first Level III method?

Yes. A first ASNT NDT Level III certificate needs the Basic plus at least one method exam, and MT qualifies.

How long should I study for MT Level III?

About 6 weeks at 6 to 8 hours a week after the Basic. Candidates adding MT to an existing Level III often need less.

Are there calculations on the MT exam?

Some. Coil L/D and ampere-turn relationships and amperage rules appear, along with questions that need you to reason about field strength and direction.

Does the exam cover both bench and yoke techniques?

Yes. Stationary bench units, portable yokes and prods, coils, central conductors and multidirectional systems are all within the body of knowledge.

How is an MT Level III certificate renewed?

Every five years, by 25 renewal points or by retaking the MT method exam.

Can I prepare for MT Level III online?

Yes. The exam is written and computer-based. Preparation runs live online, with the Practical NDT simulator available for method refresh.

Can MT and PT be prepared together?

Yes, and most candidates do. Ask for a combined MT and PT schedule.

pages.bodyHtml:
The ASNT NDT Level III liquid penetrant testing (PT) exam is a 90-question, 2-hour computer-based method exam. You need 70% to pass. With the Level III Basic, it earns an ASNT NDT Level III certificate in PT. It tests what a PT Level III must control: the capillary physics that pulls penetrant into a discontinuity, how penetrant materials are classified by type, method, sensitivity and developer form, the process variables at every step from pre-cleaning to post-cleaning, system performance checks, interpretation, and the standards and procedures a PT Level III approves. Many Level IIs think of PT as the simplest method. At Level III depth, it is a process-control exam.

Who PT Level III exam prep is for

PT is usually added alongside MT by a candidate who already holds, or is working toward, a Level III in UT or RT. The reason is practical: an employer's written practice needs Level III coverage for every method performed, and penetrant work is everywhere. Fabrication shops use it on stainless and non-magnetic welds, refineries and chemical plants on austenitic piping, and aerospace and power-generation manufacturers run fluorescent penetrant lines under tight process control.

The candidate profile splits in two. Field technicians who mostly use solvent-removable visible penetrant from aerosol cans know the basic steps but have little exposure to fluorescent lines, emulsifiers, water-wash control or system monitoring. Production-line technicians from aerospace or casting plants know process control well but may be vague on field codes and weld acceptance criteria. The exam covers both worlds, so the plan fills whichever half you are missing.

ASNT Level III PT exam structure

ItemASNT NDT Level III PT method exam
Number of questions90 multiple-choice items
Time allowed2 hours
Passing score70%
FormatComputer-based, scheduled through Pearson VUE
Also required for a first certificateASNT Level III Basic exam
Validity and renewal5 years. Renew by 25 points or by retaking the PT method exam.

Ninety questions in two hours leaves 80 seconds per item. PT questions are usually short and factual, so a well-prepared candidate finishes with time to review. The candidates who run short are the ones reasoning out classification codes from scratch.

ASNT's eligibility routes: 12 months (252 days) of NDT experience with a four-year engineering or physical science degree, 24 months (504 days) with two years of such study, or 48 months (1,008 days) with no college requirement.

What the PT Level III exam covers

We organise the ASNT PT body of knowledge, which follows the ANSI/ASNT CP-105 penetrant topical outline at Level III depth, into six domains.

1. Principles and physics

Capillary action, surface tension, wetting and contact angle, the role of viscosity in dwell time (it affects speed, not penetrating ability), fluorescence and the visible dye mechanism, and why indication brightness and contrast decide detectability. Expect conceptual questions on why a tight crack needs longer dwell, or why a contaminated surface defeats wetting.

2. Penetrant materials and classification

Type I (fluorescent) and Type II (visible) penetrants. Methods A (water-washable), B (post-emulsifiable, lipophilic), C (solvent-removable) and D (post-emulsifiable, hydrophilic). Sensitivity levels for fluorescent penetrants, and developer forms from dry powder through water-soluble, water-suspendable and nonaqueous. The exam expects you to know the classification scheme used in the aerospace-derived specifications and to choose a system for a job: a rough casting, a machined turbine part, a field weld.

3. Process steps and controls

Pre-cleaning and the damage done by mechanical cleaning that smears metal over openings (and when etching is needed), drying, penetrant application, dwell time and temperature limits, excess penetrant removal for each method (water pressure and temperature, emulsifier contact time, solvent wiping technique), drying before developer, developer application and development time, inspection conditions, and post-cleaning. A Level III sets these variables in a procedure, so questions often describe a process deviation and ask what it does to sensitivity.

4. System performance and material controls

Known-defect panels and comparator blocks, in-use checks of penetrant brightness, water content, emulsifier concentration and developer contamination, UV-A intensity and ambient light measurement, and the contaminant limits (sulfur and halogens) placed on penetrant materials used on nickel alloys, austenitic stainless steels and titanium.

5. Interpretation and evaluation

Linear versus rounded indications, bleed-out behaviour of cracks, porosity, laps, cold shuts and seams, false indications from poor washing or surface condition, and applying acceptance criteria from a code or specification.

6. Codes, standards and procedures

ASME Section V Article 6, ASTM E165 and E1417, the aerospace material specification that classifies penetrant materials (SAE AMS 2644), and what a written PT procedure must specify.

A 6-week PT Level III study plan

WeekFocusOutput
1Diagnostic; capillary physics, wetting, fluorescenceGap map
2Material classification: types, methods, sensitivity levels, developer formsClassification chart from memory
3Process steps and variables; removal methods comparedProcess-deviation scenario set
4System performance checks, in-use material controls, lighting; first timed setTimed 45-question score
5Interpretation; ASTM E165, E1417, ASME V Article 6; procedure contentDraft PT procedure outline reviewed
6Full 90-question timed mock, error-log review, second mockGo / no-go decision

Key references for the PT Level III exam

  • ASNT Nondestructive Testing Handbook, Liquid Penetrant Testing volume.
  • ASNT Level III Study Guide: Liquid Penetrant Testing.
  • ASNT Question & Answer Book for PT.
  • ANSI/ASNT CP-105 PT topical outline.
  • ASTM E165 (standard practice for liquid penetrant testing for general industry) and ASTM E1417 (standard practice for liquid penetrant testing).
  • SAE AMS 2644, the specification that classifies inspection penetrant materials.
  • ASME BPVC Section V, Article 6.

Where experienced PT technicians lose marks

  • Classification letters and numbers. Methods A to D, sensitivity levels and developer forms are easy marks if memorised and a steady loss if guessed.
  • Viscosity myths. Many technicians believe a thinner penetrant penetrates better. The exam tests the physics: viscosity governs speed of entry, while wetting and surface tension govern the ability to enter.
  • Over-removal. Questions on water pressure, temperature, emulsifier time and solvent technique test whether you understand how penetrant is removed from shallow, wide discontinuities first.
  • Surface preparation damage. Grinding, shot blasting and wire brushing can close openings. Knowing when etching is required is standard Level III content.
  • System checks. Field technicians rarely perform in-use material checks, and the exam asks about them.

Choosing a penetrant system: the Level III decision the exam keeps testing

Many PT Level III questions are system-selection questions in disguise. They describe a part, a surface and a sensitivity need and ask for the best combination of type, method and developer. Three worked examples show the reasoning we train.

A rough sand casting in a foundry. Surface roughness holds penetrant and produces background. A water-washable system is fast but can leave heavy background on rough surfaces, or be over-washed if the operator compensates. A post-emulsifiable system gives more control over removal, at the cost of an extra process step and emulsifier contact-time control. The right answer depends on the sensitivity needed and the production rate, and the exam expects you to weigh both.

A machined, high-value rotating component. Tight fatigue cracks need high sensitivity and careful removal. A fluorescent, post-emulsifiable (hydrophilic) system with a high sensitivity level and a nonaqueous or dry developer, under controlled UV-A and dark-room conditions, is the classic choice. Pre-cleaning matters as much as the penetrant: machining can smear metal over openings, which is why etching comes up.

A field weld on austenitic stainless piping. Portability and material compatibility dominate. A solvent-removable visible system is practical in the field, but the Level III must confirm the materials meet the sulfur and halogen limits for the alloy, control the temperature range, and specify solvent removal by wiping rather than flushing.

What a PT Level III controls day to day

In a production penetrant line, the Level III owns the process. That means setting dwell, emulsification and development times; defining wash water pressure and temperature; scheduling system performance checks with known-defect panels; setting in-use checks of penetrant brightness, water content in water-washable penetrants, emulsifier concentration and developer contamination; and verifying UV-A lamp output and ambient light. In field programmes the Level III approves the procedure, checks consumable batch certifications, and trains Level IIs to recognise over-removal and false indications. The Level III also writes and grades the PT Level I and II examinations under the employer's written practice. The exam's emphasis on variables, checks and classifications follows directly from those duties.

Process deviations the exam likes to test

A common Level III question describes something that went wrong on the line and asks for the likely effect. A dwell time cut short leaves tight cracks unfilled. Wash water that is too hot or at too high a pressure strips penetrant from shallow, wide discontinuities. Emulsifier left on too long makes a post-emulsifiable system behave like an over-washed water-washable one. Developer applied too thickly masks fine indications. Drying at too high a temperature degrades fluorescent brightness. A part that is still cold or hot outside the procedure's temperature range changes penetrant viscosity and behaviour. Ambient light in a fluorescent booth reduces contrast even when UV-A output is correct. None of these is exotic. Each is a variable a Level III must specify and check, and together they make up a large share of the exam.

How Atlantis PT Level III exam prep works

The course is led by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III, in live online sessions, recorded for shift workers.

  • Process-control sessions that walk through each process step as a set of variables to be specified, measured and controlled.
  • Classification drills until types, methods, sensitivity levels and developer forms are automatic.
  • Timed practice questions in the 90-question, 2-hour format with explanations, and two full mocks.
  • Procedure review of a PT procedure outline against ASME Section V Article 6 and ASTM E165 or E1417.
  • Method refresh on Practical NDT: the Practical NDT simulator, the first-ever online practical NDT simulation portal, includes penetrant scenarios in several virtual environments. It is a refresher only and does not replace hands-on work.

Request a PT Level III prep schedule. Most PT candidates also take Level III MT, and we can run both together. Our free PT Level II practice questions make a useful warm-up.

Employer sponsorship for PT Level III candidates

For employers, PT Level III coverage matters because penetrant is used on almost every job and process errors in it are easy to make and hard to spot afterwards. A PT Level III sets the process controls, approves procedures and audits in-use checks. The ASNT certificate is the credential. Under SNT-TC-1A, the employer still certifies its Level III under its own written practice. We support both sides, including a written practice review. Ask about a private PT or combined MT and PT cohort or use the training enquiry form.

ASNT Level III PT exam: frequently asked questions

How many questions are on the ASNT Level III PT exam?

90 multiple-choice questions in 2 hours, per ASNT's Level III examination listing.

What score is needed to pass?

70%.

Is PT Level III just the Level II material again?

No. It goes much deeper into capillary physics, material classification, process variables and system performance checks, the controls a Level III sets and audits.

Does the exam cover fluorescent penetrant lines?

Yes. Fluorescent systems, emulsifiers, water-wash controls, UV-A lighting and in-use checks all appear, even for candidates who only use visible penetrant in the field.

How long should I study for PT Level III?

About 6 weeks at 6 to 8 hours a week after the Basic. It is shorter if you are studying it straight after MT.

Can PT be my first Level III method?

Yes. Basic plus the PT method exam gives an ASNT NDT Level III certificate in PT.

Which standards should I read?

ASME Section V Article 6, ASTM E165, ASTM E1417 and SAE AMS 2644, alongside the ASNT handbook volume and study guide.

How is a PT Level III certificate renewed?

Every five years, by 25 renewal points or by retaking the PT method exam.

Can I prepare online?

Yes. The exam is written and computer-based, and our preparation runs live online.

Can my company book a group?

Yes. Send candidate numbers and target dates for a quote within one business day.
